name: Lapse Capital: a land bank built on expired survey data
pitch: This company never flies a survey. Saskatchewan's own Airborne Surveys layer lists 1,831 company-flown surveys. 615 are post-2000, and 335 of those are helicopter EM totalling about 395,000 line-km. At US$125-200/lkm, replacing that archive would cost about US$50-80M (estimate). Section 68 of the Mineral Tenure Registry Regulations makes the raw contractor data public at the earliest of three years after filing or the claim lapsing. So the signal is released at the moment its owner gives up the ground. ML levels, merges and re-inverts these files into one claim-indexed conductor model of the Athabasca. Greenridge's 2026 parametric re-inversion of a 2014 VTEM survey found more than 15 km of untested strike without any new flying, which is the proof case. The company re-stakes lapsed or open ground at staking cost, roughly C$0.60-15/ha (estimate). It then vends that ground to capitalised optionees, whose Athabasca earn-ins typically run C$3-15M of spend plus C$0.1-1M in cash and shares (estimate), and it keeps a 1-3% NSR. The same pipeline extends to BC ARIS (1-year confidentiality), Manitoba (3 years), Ontario (85,000+ assessment files, C$0-25 per dataset), Alberta and Quebec.
what_it_owns: Re-staked claims over legacy-proven conductor corridors; equity received from optionees; retained 1-3% NSRs (estimate); a proprietary merged, re-inverted conductor model across provinces (a data moat, but the ground is the asset).
why_ml_is_the_lever: The data exists but cannot be read at scale. About 600 digital surveys from different contractors and systems (VTEM, ZTEM, AeroTEM, HeliTEM and others) sit unlevelled on DVDs. About 1,118 pre-1990 INPUT EM and radiometric surveys exist only as scanned maps. Ingesting them takes vision models to digitise the scans, ML levelling and cross-system merging, and fast surrogate-model inversion run on every off-confidentiality survey the day it lapses. Done by hand, that is consultancy work (CGI, Mira) at bespoke prices. Done by ML, it is a pipeline. On the gold rubric: C1 is strong, because the physical step is staking (trivial) and the cost of the information step is zero flight. C2 is strong in uranium, since earn-in partners pay for the 'ranked conductor corridors' state. C3 is ML on re-inversion and ranking, a plausible 1.5-3x improvement in which re-staked ground yields drill-worthy conductors. C4 is the best fit of the four: public but illegible data, released exactly when the right is cheap. C5 runs prospect generator to royalty company to JV operator. The ceiling is the weak point. Survey-stage value is modest (raw block about C$50-300k rising to about C$0.3-1.5M once conductors are ranked; estimate). Venture scale therefore depends on keeping NSRs and equity through to discovery (Fission went for about C$1.1B; unverified) and on running many provinces and countries. Headwind: the 2024 rule (SR 62/2024) credits new airborne spend at 1.5x for assessment purposes, and it is unverified whether reprocessing legacy data earns any credit.
prospecting_rule_note: This is plainly a prospecting / prospect-generator idea. It sits inside the founder's earlier 'no prospecting' exclusion, and it overlaps heavily with Terranox's own model (ML on SMAD, then buy rights). It differs in using the geophysics archive rather than assessment text, and in skipping the survey entirely. Flag that it may read as a Terranox feature rather than a new company.

name: Speculative Fly-First, Stake-First Multi-Client Surveys (privatising the QUEST effect)
pitch: Geoscience BC's QUEST program spent about C$5M on helicopter VTEM and gravity over about 46,000 km² and released the data free. It stakes the best 5-10% of the ground before anyone else sees the data. It then monetises three ways: (a) vending staked blocks that come with conductors, (b) selling multi-client data licences on the unstaked remainder to juniors and majors on the TGS model (TGS: US$883.8M multi-client sales against US$446.8M investment in FY2025, a 2.0x sales-to-investment ratio), and (c) selling discounted pooled slots to juniors whose existing claims fall inside the block. what_it_owns: It owns the survey data outright, since it is flown speculatively and stays proprietary on unstaked ground until the company chooses otherwise. The data library compounds through vintage sales; TGS's Q4 2025 was driven by 'healthy sales of vintage data'.

- **Saskatchewan airborne addressable market:** about C$10-30M/yr (estimate). Context: Saskatchewan exploration spend was C$561.6M in 2024. There is no Saskatchewan subsidy for airborne work; TMEI covers ground geophysics only.
- **Global airborne services:** US$1.06-1.5B/yr. Aeroquest's gross margin fell to 11.6%, and Geotech bought it for C$5.6M after a roughly 90% value collapse.

- The physical step (the helicopter) **is** the information step. It is not abstracted away the way drilling is for Terranox.

- The prospect-generator model is proven: optionees pay cash, work commitments, equity and an NSR for conductor-ranked ground (EMX, Eagle Plains, Skyharbour, CanAlaska).
- But the proven state at this rung is "conductor," not "drill hit." The step-up is roughly 10-100x on staking cost (estimate), against Terranox's 10^4.

- Line selection from a basin prior plus legacy geophysics might raise the speculative-line hit rate 1.5-2x (estimate).

- The economics close without ML, because brokers and contractors already piggyback blocks. ML is a nice-to-have here, and it fails the founder's "ML must make it solvable" test.

### C4 = 2: public-but-illegible signal plus a cheap unproven right
- The signal is freshly acquired proprietary data, not illegible public data. That is the opposite of the Terranox edge.
- The cheap right (Crown staking) is real, but prime open Athabasca ground is scarce after the 2023-25 staking rush (inference).

### C5 = 3: ladder toward the whole chain
- The ladder is coherent: broker, then fleet (drone passive EM such as MobileMTd, which is still a prototype), then land bank, then operator.
- Every rung is capital-heavy and cyclical.
- Xcalibur already sits on the fleet and multi-client rungs with PE money.

### Bottom line
The best part of the idea is capturing the land-rush value that free government surveys hand away. But that value accrues mostly to whoever stakes fastest, which is a staking-speed and capital game, not an ML moat. It also competes with free government data and with self-flying majors. It prices them on today's poor knowledge of the subsurface, then flies heli or drone AEM to prove storage volume, aquifer continuity and recharge pathways. The proven asset is sold or leased to the capitalised buyers who pay for certainty: municipal utilities, data-centre developers with water constraints, agriculture, and managed-aquifer-recharge and water-banking programs. ## Verdict: 10/25. This is a weak fit. The rubric breaks at C1, because the hard part of proving water value is legal and political, not information.

**Research caveat:** the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) was used up before this scorer ran. My three verification searches (Vidler deal price, Cadiz financials, private AEM-led water acquirers) returned nothing. Figures below come from the supplied research summary (sourced there) or from my prior knowledge; anything not in the summary is marked (estimate/unverified). A follow-up turn could verify Vidler/Cadiz/WAM numbers.

### C1 = 1.5/5 (information step 80%+, physical step trivial)
- Survey cost is cheap relative to the asset: helicopter AEM costs US$150-500/lkm (Nebraska guideline caps all-in at US$500/lkm), and basin surveys run US$0.1-1M. That part holds.
- But AEM gives resistivity, i.e. a lithology proxy (clay vs sand/gravel). It does not give yield, water quality, recharge rate or legal pumpable volume.
- Proving a saleable supply still takes test wells, pumping tests, water-quality sampling, environmental review (CEQA/NEPA), GSA approval and often court adjudication. I estimate that is 60-80% of the cost and time. So the 'proof' rung is mostly a regulatory and physical step, which is the opposite of Terranox.
- Uranium is different. There a drill hit converts land from $1/ha to $10,000/ha because mineral title already covers whatever you find. A water right's value is set by priority date and permitted quantity, not by aquifer size under the parcel.

### C2 = 2.5/5 (a capitalised buyer pays a step-up at that rung)
- Capitalised buyers are real: municipal utilities, homebuilders (D.R. Horton bought Vidler for about US$290M, unverified), data centres, and ag-to-urban transfer buyers (Water Asset Management).
- Big spreads exist. Colorado River and Front Range urban rights can reach US$20-50k per acre-foot vs roughly US$1-5k for ag rights (estimate). The spread comes from **transfer approval** (an ag-to-urban change of use), not from subsurface knowledge.
- No buyer pays a step-up for 'AEM-proven storage' by itself. Managed aquifer recharge and water banking (Kern Water Bank, Semitropic) do value storage capacity, but they need recharge water rights plus conveyance plus permits. The SGMA 'tradable storage credit' idea is mostly speculative: only a handful of basins (e.g. some Kern and Mojave adjudicated markets) have functioning groundwater credit trading.
- Partial credit: buyers exist, but the step-up is not tied to the information rung.

### C3 = 1.5/5 (ML/software lever on hit rate or cost)
- AEM inversion into hydrostratigraphy is already semi-automated, and the incumbents are adding ML: EMerald Geomodelling (ML AEM interpretation) was acquired by Xcalibur in March 2026, alongside Aqua Geo Frameworks and I-GIS/Aarhus Workbench.
- Parcel screening from well logs, InSAR and land prices is useful. But the 'hit rate' that matters is whether a transfer or permit gets approved, which ML barely moves.
- My estimate of the lever on realised value is at most about 1.2-1.5x. ML is a nice-to-have here, not what makes the problem solvable.

### C4 = 2/5 (signal in public-but-illegible data, plus a cheaply bought right)
- The arbitrage is real, but it is legal and market illegibility, not subsurface illegibility. Rural rights trade on informal local pricing, and title and priority records are messy county and state filings. An LLM-based rights/title-parsing play is more interesting than the AEM play.
- The geophysical data is not illegible. California DWR publishes its ~16,000 line-mile AEM survey free with interpreted products, USGS Earth MRI is public, and SkyTEM/Danish data is fully public. Basin storage in SGMA basins is already characterised in Groundwater Sustainability Plans, so the information edge from re-inverting public AEM is thin.
- Cheaply bought rights exist (dry-land ag parcels, junior rights), but a junior right in an over-drafted basin is cheap because it is legally weak, and AEM doesn't fix that.

### C5 = 2.5/5 (ladder toward the whole chain)
- The ladder is coherent: rights aggregator, then banking/MAR operator, then regulated utility or infrastructure owner. Precedents are Cadiz, Pure Cycle and Texas Pacific Land's water segment (about US$150M+/yr revenue, estimate).
- But regulated utility returns are capped (about 9-10% ROE), transfers face anti-export politics (Imperial Valley, Owens Valley history), and Cadiz shows 25+ years of litigation with little revenue. This is a slow, capital-intensive infrastructure path, not a trillion-dollar discovery engine.

### Ceiling and value ownership
- Owning rights does let you capture value rather than sell services, which fits the rubric's preference.
- But the AEM-attributable slice is small. The groundwater AEM services market is about US$30-80M/yr (estimate), and water-rights realised value in the target basins is perhaps US$0.3-1B/yr for a dominant player (estimate).
- What scales is a water-rights merchant/fund (Water Asset Management-style), which is a finance business where geophysics is incidental.

### Prospecting-rule note
This is subsurface prospecting in spirit: it uses surveys to find and prove a buried resource. It is the most distinct idea from Terranox. But it is also the one where the Terranox insight transfers worst, because a mineral claim gives you title to what you find, while a water right is defined by law and the aquifer is a shared commons.

### If kept, the pivot
Drop 'prove with AEM' as the core. Instead, use ML/LLM to parse fragmented water-right title, priority and transfer records across western states (the real illegible public data), and buy ag rights with high transfer-approval probability near urban or data-centre demand. That makes C2 and C4 stronger, but C1 still depends on regulators, so it would score about 13-14/25 at best (estimate).
